title: Lewis Symbols and Structures
lead: A Lewis symbol shows the valence electrons of an atom or a monatomic ion as dots around its symbol, and a Lewis structure shows how the valence electrons of a molecule or polyatomic ion are shared in bonds or held as lone pairs. The octet rule guides how these structures are written, with single, double and triple bonds, and some central atoms break it.
objectives: Write Lewis symbols for neutral atoms and ions
Draw Lewis structures depicting the bonding in simple molecules
summary_html: Valence electronic structures can be visualized by drawing Lewis symbols (for atoms and monatomic ions) and Lewis structures (for molecules and polyatomic ions). Lone pairs, unpaired electrons, and single, double, or triple bonds are used to indicate where the valence electrons are located around each atom in a Lewis structure. Most structures—especially those containing second row elements—obey the octet rule, in which every atom (except H) is surrounded by eight electrons. Exceptions to the octet rule occur for odd-electron molecules (free radicals), electron-deficient molecules, and hypervalent molecules.

exercises.prompt:
Many monatomic ions are found in seawater, including the ions formed from the following list of elements. Write the Lewis symbols for the monatomic ions formed from the following elements:
(a) Cl
(b) Na
(c) Mg
(d) Ca
(e) K
(f) Br
(g) Sr
(h) F

answer.solution:
Metal atoms lose all their valence electrons, so their cations are drawn with no dots; nonmetal atoms gain electrons until they have eight, so their anions are drawn with eight dots in brackets, with the charge outside.
(a) Cl–: Cl with eight dots (four pairs) in brackets, charge –. A chlorine atom has seven valence electrons and gains one.
(b) Na+: Na with no dots. The atom loses its one valence electron.
(c) Mg2+: Mg with no dots. The atom loses its two valence electrons.
(d) Ca2+: Ca with no dots. The atom loses its two valence electrons.
(e) K+: K with no dots. The atom loses its one valence electron.
(f) Br–: Br with eight dots in brackets, charge –. A bromine atom has seven valence electrons and gains one.
(g) Sr2+: Sr with no dots. The atom loses its two valence electrons.
(h) F–: F with eight dots in brackets, charge –. A fluorine atom has seven valence electrons and gains one.

exercises.prompt:
In the Lewis structures listed here, M and X represent various elements in the third period of the periodic table. Write the formula of each compound using the chemical symbols of each element:
(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

answer.solution:
(a) MgS. (b) AlCl3. (c) Na2S. (d) Al2S3. In the third period, a cation with no dots and charge 1+, 2+ or 3+ comes from Na, Mg or Al, whose atoms lose one, two or three valence electrons. An anion with eight dots and charge 1– or 2– comes from Cl or S, whose atoms gain one or two electrons to reach eight. A subscript outside the brackets gives the number of that ion.
(a) One M2+ is Mg2+ and one X2– is S2–, so the compound is MgS.
(b) One M3+ is Al3+ and three X– are three Cl–, so it is AlCl3.
(c) Two M+ are two Na+ and one X2– is S2–, so it is Na2S.
(d) Two M3+ are two Al3+ and three X2– are three S2–, so it is Al2S3. In each, the positive and negative charges cancel.

Write Lewis structures for the following:
(a) H2
(b) HBr
(c) PCl3
(d) SF2
(e) H2CCH2
(f) HNNH
(g) H2CNH
(h) NO–
(i) N2
(j) CO
(k) CN–

answer.solution:
Each structure uses exactly the valence electrons counted for it and gives every atom an octet, or two electrons for hydrogen.
(a) H2, 2 electrons: H–H, one single bond and no lone pairs.
(b) HBr, 1 + 7 = 8 electrons: H–Br, with three lone pairs on Br.
(c) PCl3, 5 + 3(7) = 26 electrons: P in the center joined to three Cl atoms by single bonds, three lone pairs on each Cl and one lone pair on P.
(d) SF2, 6 + 2(7) = 20 electrons: F–S–F with single bonds, three lone pairs on each F and two lone pairs on S.
(e) H2CCH2, 2(4) + 4(1) = 12 electrons: a C=C double bond, each carbon also bonded to two H atoms, no lone pairs.
(f) HNNH, 2(1) + 2(5) = 12 electrons: H–N=N–H, with one lone pair on each N.
(g) H2CNH, 4 + 5 + 3(1) = 12 electrons: a C=N double bond, carbon bonded to two H atoms, nitrogen bonded to one H atom and carrying one lone pair.
(h) NO–, 5 + 6 + 1 = 12 electrons: N=O, with two lone pairs on N and two on O, in brackets with charge –.
(i) N2, 2(5) = 10 electrons: N≡N, with one lone pair on each N.
(j) CO, 4 + 6 = 10 electrons: C≡O, with one lone pair on each atom.
(k) CN–, 4 + 5 + 1 = 10 electrons: C≡N, with one lone pair on each atom, in brackets with charge –.
In (e) through (k), single bonds left an atom short of an octet, so lone pairs of a neighbor were moved into double or triple bonds, as for NO+ and HCN.

exercises.prompt:
Write Lewis structures for the following:
(a) ClF3
(b) PCl5
(c) BF3
(d) ${\text{PF}}_{6}{}^{\text{−}}$

answer.solution:
(a) ClF3, 7 + 3(7) = 28 electrons: Cl in the center with three Cl–F single bonds, three lone pairs on each F, and the 4 electrons left over as two lone pairs on Cl. Chlorine has 10 electrons, which a third-period atom can hold.
(b) PCl5, 5 + 5(7) = 40 electrons: P in the center with five P–Cl single bonds and three lone pairs on each Cl. No electrons remain, and phosphorus shares five pairs, 10 electrons, as in Figure 7.12.
(c) BF3, 3 + 3(7) = 24 electrons: B in the center with three B–F single bonds and three lone pairs on each F. Boron has only 6 electrons; it is electron deficient, and the structure with three single bonds is the best one, as the measured bond lengths show.
(d) ${\text{PF}}_{6}{}^{\text{−}}$, 5 + 6(7) + 1 = 48 electrons: P in the center with six P–F single bonds and three lone pairs on each F, all in brackets with charge –. No electrons remain, and phosphorus has 12 electrons, like sulfur in SF6.

exercises.prompt:
Write Lewis structures for:
(a) ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}$
(b) ${\text{ICl}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}$
(c) ${\text{SO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}$
(d) HONO

answer.solution:
(a) ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}$, 5 + 4(6) + 3 = 32 electrons: P in the center with four P–O single bonds and three lone pairs on each O, in brackets with charge 3–. Every atom has an octet.
(b) ${\text{ICl}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}$, 7 + 4(7) + 1 = 36 electrons: I in the center with four I–Cl single bonds and three lone pairs on each Cl, using 32 electrons. The other 4 go on iodine as two lone pairs, so iodine holds 12 electrons, as xenon does in XeF4. The structure is in brackets with charge –.
(c) ${\text{SO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}$, 6 + 3(6) + 2 = 26 electrons: S in the center with three S–O single bonds and three lone pairs on each O, using 24 electrons. The last 2 go on sulfur as one lone pair, completing its octet. The structure is in brackets with charge 2–.
(d) HONO, 1 + 2(6) + 5 = 18 electrons: H–O–N=O. The middle oxygen carries two lone pairs, nitrogen one lone pair and the terminal oxygen two lone pairs. With single bonds only, nitrogen had just 6 electrons, so one lone pair of the terminal oxygen became the N=O double bond.

exercises.prompt: Correct the following statement: “The bonds in solid PbCl<sub>2</sub> are ionic; the bond in a HCl molecule is covalent. Thus, all of the valence electrons in PbCl<sub>2</sub> are located on the Cl<sup>–</sup> ions, and all of the valence electrons in a HCl molecule are shared between the H and Cl atoms.”

answer.solution: Two valence electrons per Pb atom are transferred to Cl atoms; the resulting Pb2+ ion has a 6s2 valence shell configuration. Two of the valence electrons in the HCl molecule are shared, and the other six are located on the Cl atom as lone pairs of electrons.

exercises.prompt:
Write Lewis structures for the following molecules or ions:
(a) SbH3
(b) XeF2
(c) Se8 (a cyclic molecule with a ring of eight Se atoms)

answer.solution:
(a) SbH3, 5 + 3(1) = 8 electrons: Sb in the center with three Sb–H single bonds and one lone pair on Sb, the same pattern as NH3, since antimony is in group 15.
(b) XeF2, 8 + 2(7) = 22 electrons: F–Xe–F with single bonds, three lone pairs on each F and the remaining 6 electrons as three lone pairs on Xe. Xenon holds 10 electrons, as in Example 7.5.
(c) Se8, 8(6) = 48 electrons: eight Se atoms in a ring joined by eight Se–Se single bonds, which use 16 electrons. The other 32 electrons are two lone pairs on each Se atom, so every atom has two bonds and two lone pairs, an octet, as an oxygen atom does in water.

exercises.prompt: Methanol, H<sub>3</sub>COH, is used as the fuel in some race cars. Ethanol, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, is used extensively as motor fuel in Brazil. Both methanol and ethanol produce CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O when they burn. Write the chemical equations for these combustion reactions using Lewis structures instead of chemical formulas.

Many planets in our solar system contain organic chemicals including methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and traces of ethylene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>), ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), propyne (H<sub>3</sub>CCCH), and diacetylene (HCCCCH). Write the Lewis structures for each of these molecules.

answer.solution:
Carbon forms four bonds and hydrogen one, and each structure uses all the valence electrons.
Methane, CH4, 4 + 4(1) = 8 electrons: C in the center with four C–H single bonds.
Ethylene, C2H4, 2(4) + 4(1) = 12 electrons: H2C=CH2, a carbon-carbon double bond with two H atoms on each carbon.
Ethane, C2H6, 2(4) + 6(1) = 14 electrons: H3C–CH3, all single bonds, three H atoms on each carbon.
Propyne, H3CCCH, 3(4) + 4(1) = 16 electrons: H3C–C≡C–H, a CH3 group joined by a single bond to a carbon that is triple bonded to a carbon carrying one H.
Diacetylene, HCCCCH, 4(4) + 2(1) = 18 electrons: H–C≡C–C≡C–H, two triple bonds joined by a single bond.
None of the structures has lone pairs. In ethylene, propyne and diacetylene, single bonds alone leave carbon atoms short of an octet, so their electrons form double or triple bonds, as in acetylene in Example 7.4.

exercises.prompt: Carbon tetrachloride was formerly used in fire extinguishers for electrical fires. It is no longer used for this purpose because of the formation of the toxic gas phosgene, Cl<sub>2</sub>CO. Write the Lewis structures for carbon tetrachloride and phosgene.

Identify the atoms that correspond to each of the following electron configurations. Then, write the Lewis symbol for the common ion formed from each atom:
(a) 1s22s22p5
(b) 1s22s22p63s2
(c) 1s22s22p63s23p64s23d10
(d) 1s22s22p63s23p64s23d104p4
(e) 1s22s22p63s23p64s23d104p1

answer.solution:
The number of electrons in each configuration is the atomic number of the atom. A metal atom loses its valence electrons, giving a cation drawn with no dots, and a nonmetal atom gains enough electrons to reach eight, giving an anion drawn with eight dots in brackets.
(a) 9 electrons: fluorine. A fluorine atom has seven valence electrons and gains one, so its ion is F–, drawn with eight dots in brackets and the charge –.
(b) 12 electrons: magnesium. The atom loses its two 3s electrons, so its ion is Mg2+, drawn with no dots.
(c) 30 electrons: zinc. The atom loses its two 4s electrons, so its ion is Zn2+, drawn with no dots.
(d) 34 electrons: selenium. Its six valence electrons, 4s24p4, become eight when it gains two, so its ion is Se2–, drawn with eight dots in brackets and the charge 2–.
(e) 31 electrons: gallium. The atom loses its three valence electrons, 4s24p1, so its ion is Ga3+, drawn with no dots.

exercises.prompt: A compound with a molar mass of about 42 g/mol contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Write the Lewis structure for a molecule of the compound.
How are single, double, and triple bonds similar? How do they differ?

answer.solution: Each bond includes a sharing of electrons between atoms. Two electrons are shared in a single bond; four electrons are shared in a double bond; and six electrons are shared in a triple bond.
